item.title: Self-Hosted PAM Authentication Modules: Google Authenticator vs pam_u2f vs pam_oath vs pam_duo
item.description:
Introduction

Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) form the backbone of Linux authentication. Every SSH login, sudo invocation, and system service authentication flows through PAM’s modular stack. While the default pam_unix module handles basic password authentication, modern security requirements demand multi-factor authentication (MFA), hardware token support, and push-based verification.

item.title: Self-Hosted PAM Multi-Factor Authentication: pam-u2f vs Google Authenticator PAM vs libpam-oath
item.description: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is essential for securing self-hosted servers, but most organizations rely on cloud-based MFA services like Duo, Okta, or Azure MFA. For fully self-hosted infrastructure, PAM (Pluggable Authentication Module) provides MFA capabilities without external dependencies. In this guide, we compare three open-source PAM MFA modules: pam-u2f (FIDO2/U2F hardware keys), Google Authenticator PAM (TOTP time-based codes), and libpam-oath (OATH HOTP/TOTP protocols) — evaluating their security models, deployment complexity, and user experience.

item.title: Self-Hosted PAM Management: SSSD vs libpam-pwquality vs pam-auth-update Configuration Guide
item.description: Linux Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) control how users authenticate to every service on a system — SSH, sudo, login, graphical sessions, and custom applications. Managing PAM configuration manually is error-prone: a single typo can lock you out of the system. PAM management tools automate configuration, enforce password policies, and centralize authentication across distributed Linux servers.
